items.text: Autistic burnout isn't just exhaustion. Research is finally naming what the community already knew: it's an identity collapse. You don't just run out of energy — you lose track of who you are.
items.rationale: Opens with the community's existing knowledge, then adds the research layer without being clinical. 'Identity collapse' is the specific undernamed finding from the 2026 qualitative study — more precise and landing than 'burnout is real.'

items.text: New research on autistic burnout finds that what makes it devastating isn't tiredness — it's shame. The sense that you've failed at being a person, not just at keeping up.
items.rationale: Leads directly with the research finding. 'Failed at being a person' names the specific texture of the shame layer the 2026 study identifies — visceral and recognizable without clinical language.

items.text: Nobody warned me that getting diagnosed would mean grieving. Not the autism — the years I spent calling myself lazy, broken, too much.
items.rationale: First-person 'I' voice makes this direct and human. Names the specific grief objects (lazy, broken, too much) that resonate for late-diagnosed adults. Short, sharp, no setup needed.

items.text: Late diagnosis brings relief and grief at the same time. They're not opposites. You can be grateful for finally understanding yourself and be devastated for the kid who didn't know.
items.rationale: Challenges the dominant 'relief' narrative by naming the coexistence — drawn from the Grief/Relief/Belief cycle study. 'The kid who didn't know' is specific and lands harder than 'your younger self.'

items.text: Using AI to write emails that sound neurotypical. Noise-cancelling to survive the office. Useful — until it makes you invisible to the people who could actually support you.
items.rationale: Opens with concrete, recognizable behavior before landing the counterintuitive cost. The 'useful — until' pivot is the whole insight, delivered fast. Drawn directly from the 2026 Wiley study on neurodivergent workers and AT.

items.text: Assistive tech at work can help neurodivergent people pass. That's both the win and the trap. The people who could accommodate you can't support what they can't see.
items.rationale: Reframes the tool as double-edged without being preachy. 'Pass' is a deliberately loaded word the community will recognize. Ends on the systemic tension, not a personal failing. Observational, not prescriptive about disclosure.

items.text: PDA isn't a child choosing to refuse. It's a nervous system already on fire, responding to one more spark. The demand isn't the problem — the threat signal is.
items.rationale: Clean three-sentence structure: old frame, new frame, implication. 'Already on fire' is visceral and specific. Centers the nervous system response rather than naming the child as broken.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't letting your child run the house. It's deciding the relationship and their nervous system matter more right now than winning the sock argument.
items.rationale: 'The sock argument' is specific and faintly funny — instantly recognizable to any parent who's been there. Draws the distinction cleanly without requiring the reader to know the research or the terminology.

items.text: Nobody talks about what it costs to hold low-demand space for your PDA kid when your own nervous system is also screaming. You're not failing at the approach. You're doing it empty.
items.rationale: Speaks directly to the AuDHD parent experience with almost no content representation elsewhere. 'Doing it empty' is the right note — not a verdict on failure, but an acknowledgment of real, compounded depletion.

items.text: ADHD executive dysfunction isn't a willpower problem. It's a fit problem. The question isn't 'why can't I just do this?' — it's 'what would the right conditions look like?'
items.rationale: Moves past the worn 'not laziness' framing into the actionable next step: design over self-blame. The contrast between the two questions carries the whole insight and gives readers something to actually do with it.

items.text: 'Why can't I just do this?' is a moral question. 'What conditions would make this possible?' is a design question. For ADHD minds, one of those is worth asking.
items.rationale: Aphoristic companion to the prior ADHD reframe but structurally different — paired sentences, dryer tone. The final line respects the reader's intelligence by not spelling out the obvious conclusion.

items.text: For those who've come back from autistic burnout — not just managing but actually rebuilt some capacity — what actually helped? Not the advice. What worked for you, specifically?
items.rationale: 'Not the advice' signals this is a genuine ask, not a setup for a listicle. 'Specifically' does the same work. Open-ended, non-prescriptive, and invites the kind of discussion that builds community rather than collecting passive likes.
